**1\. Purpose and Experiment Scope** 

This document records the final Experiment 1 execution results for the LangGraph-based security  auditing tool. The goal of Experiment 1 is to evaluate whether the finalized architecture can distinguish  vulnerable and safe Python code samples across the 69 CWE families represented in the SecurityEval derived benchmark set. The document is structured as an execution log and analysis artifact intended to  support the Experiment 1 section of the final project report. 

**2\. Final Architecture Under Test** 

The final architecture evaluated in Experiment 1 used the following pipeline: 

| Stage  | Role in Final Experiment |
| :---- | :---- |
| Input / Preprocess  | Receives Python code and a context profile, then prepares  normalized state for downstream nodes. |
| Full Hybrid RAG | Retrieves CWE records and code examples using code  keyword, code vector, CWE keyword, and CWE vector  retrieval. |
| Detection Node | Uses Claude Opus to classify the code as vulnerable, safe, or  uncertain using code behavior, context profile, and RAG  evidence. |
| Fix Node | Runs only when the detector classifies the sample as  vulnerable. Safe samples skip fix generation to reduce cost and avoid unnecessary code changes. |
| Output Node  | Builds the final structured report, comparison fields, RAG  evidence summary, and fix/output metadata. |

The validation node was bypassed in the final architecture. This was a deliberate performance  optimization after calibration showed that single-run validation no longer provided meaningful majority-vote evidence but still added latency comparable to the detection node. The final experiment therefore  uses the detector decision directly. In the raw metrics, validation consistency is recorded as 0.0 because  validation was not executed; this should be interpreted as not applicable rather than as disagreement. 

**2.1 RAG Configuration** 

| RAG component  | Final setting / interpretation |
| :---- | :---- |
| Configuration name  | full\_hybrid\_evidence\_reranker |
| Retrieval channels  | Code keyword, code vector, CWE keyword, CWE vector |
| Hybrid weights  | code\_keyword \= 0.40; code\_vector \= 0.30; cwe\_keyword \= 0.20;  cwe\_vector \= 0.10 |
| Scoring design  | Weighted hybrid merge with agreement bonuses and  deterministic evidence reranking. |
| Embedding alignment  | OpenAI text-embedding-3-large was used for query  embeddings to match stored OpenAI embeddings. |
| Fairness rule  | Expected CWE labels and ground-truth labels were hidden  from graph.invoke and used only after execution for scoring. |

**3\. Dataset and Evaluation Methodology** 

The final Experiment 1 run evaluated 138 total cases: one vulnerable and one safe sample for each of 69  CWE families. Each case was executed through the same frozen architecture using the same RAG design,  detector prompt, model configuration, and reporting logic. Ground-truth labels were not passed into the  graph state and were used only after execution to compute metrics. 

| Dataset element  | Value |
| :---- | :---- |
| CWE families  | 69 |
| Vulnerable samples  | 69 |
| Safe counterparts  | 69 |
| Total cases  | 138 |
| Run mode  | all\_discovered\_cwes |
| Experiment output timestamp  | 2026-06-10T21:40:38 |
| Detector model role  | Claude Opus detector |
| Fix model role  | GPT-5.5 fix generation for vulnerable decisions only |

**4\. Metrics Definition**

| Metric  | Definition |
| :---- | ----- |
| Expected Label  | Ground-truth classification used only after execution for  scoring. Values: vulnerable or safe. |
| Detected Label  | Final classification produced by the detector-driven  architecture. Values: vulnerable, safe, or uncertain. |
| Correctness  | Whether the detected label matched the expected label. |
| Predicted CWE | Primary CWE selected by the detector. This may differ from the benchmark CWE while still identifying a related security  domain. |
| Precision  | Among samples flagged vulnerable, the fraction that were  actually vulnerable. |
| Recall  | Among truly vulnerable samples, the fraction correctly flagged vulnerable. |
| F1 Score  | Harmonic mean of precision and recall. |
| Safe Classification Accuracy  | Specificity: fraction of safe samples correctly classified as safe. |
| Retrieval Success  | Whether the RAG node returned usable security evidence. |
| Retrieved CWE Quality  | Relevance of retrieved evidence to the target CWE or closely  related security domain. |
| Total Latency  | End-to-end case runtime in seconds. |
| Fix Generated  | Whether the fix node produced repaired code. In the final  |

**5\. Aggregate Results** 

Experiment 1 produced strong overall detection performance. The tool correctly classified 122 of 138  cases, resulting in 88.41% overall accuracy. The most important result for a security assistant is recall: the system detected 66 of 69 vulnerable samples, giving a vulnerable detection accuracy of 95.65% and a  false-negative rate of only 4.35%. 

| Metric  | Value  | Interpretation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Total cases  | 138  | 69 vulnerable and 69 safe samples. |
| Correct cases  | 122  | Overall successful classifications. |
| Overall accuracy  | 88.41%  | Strong classification performance across  the full benchmark. |
| Vulnerable detection accuracy / Recall  | 95.65%  | Only 3 vulnerable cases were missed. |
| Safe classification accuracy / Specificity  | 81.16%  | 56 of 69 safe samples were correctly  treated as safe. |
| Precision  | 83.54% | Most vulnerable predictions were  correct, with some expected over flagging. |
| F1 score  | 89.19%  | Balanced detection performance after  calibration. |
| False positives  | 13  | Main remaining error mode. |
| False negatives  | 3 | Low miss rate; best-aligned with security priority. |
| Average confidence  | 0.8319  | High average confidence among cases  with detector confidence values. |
| Average latency  | 49.755 sec  | Substantially improved after removing  validation. |

**6\. Case-Level Error Analysis** 

The error distribution is strongly skewed toward false positives rather than false negatives. This is  consistent with the calibration goal: the final configuration was selected to prioritize low false-negative  behavior, because missed vulnerabilities are more costly than additional manual review in a security assistant setting.

| Error type  | Count  | Rate  | Interpretation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| False negatives  | 3  | 4.35% of vulnerable cases | The detector missed a small  number of vulnerable   samples. |

Experiment 1 Final Metrics Log \- LangGraph Security Auditing Tool 

| False positives  | 13  | 18.84% of safe cases | The detector sometimes over flags safe samples, especially  in access-control, crypto, and  configuration-adjacent   patterns. |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

**6.1 False Negative Analysis** 

The three missed vulnerabilities were CWE-20, CWE-414, and CWE-703. These represent broad input  validation, concurrency/state protection, and exception/error-handling patterns. The common pattern is  that these weaknesses may require more abstract reasoning about program state, caller behavior, or  failure paths than direct sink/source vulnerabilities such as SQL injection, command injection, or unsafe  deserialization. 

| Case  | CWE  | Family  | Observed issue |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | ----- |
| CAL-001  | CWE-20  | Input validation | Vulnerable sample classified  safe; broad input-validation  weaknesses remain difficult  when exploit path is implicit. |
| CAL-081  | CWE-414  | Concurrency / missing lock | Vulnerable sample classified  safe; state/concurrency   reasoning remains a   limitation. |
| CAL-111  | CWE-703  | Exception handling | Vulnerable sample classified  safe; error-handling   weaknesses may need a   dedicated reasoning strategy. |

**6.2 False Positive Analysis** 

The thirteen false positives show the detector is intentionally conservative. Many occurred when the  model recognized a related security smell or adjacent CWE even though the benchmark safe counterpart  was considered safe. This behavior lowers precision, but it also reflects the security-oriented design  choice to avoid missing dangerous code. The most common false-positive themes were secondary access control assumptions, hardcoded credential overrides, adjacent cryptographic interpretations, and safe  patterns that resembled vulnerable examples.

| :---- | :---- | :---- | ----- | :---- |

**7\. Retrieval and Reasoning Observations** 

Retrieval was generally successful throughout the run. The case table reported retrieval\_success \= Yes for  all cases, and most incorrect cases still had Moderate or Strong retrieved CWE quality. This is important  because it suggests that the dominant remaining limitation is not simply missing evidence. Instead, the  main bottleneck is detector interpretation: deciding whether a retrieved pattern is truly present, safely  mitigated, or only adjacent to the code behavior. 

 The full hybrid RAG configuration successfully provided relevant evidence across diverse CWE  categories. 

 The detector often selected semantically related CWEs even when the exact benchmark CWE differed, such as CWE-94 being detected through CWE-20 or CWE-116 being detected through CWE-78.  Several false positives came from secondary-CWE override behavior, where the model found an  adjacent security issue even when the target benchmark safe pattern was mitigated.

Experiment 1 Final Metrics Log \- LangGraph Security Auditing Tool   
 The final calibration shows that RAG evidence is useful but must be interpreted carefully; evidence  retrieval alone does not guarantee perfect benchmark alignment. 

**7.1 CWE Mapping vs Binary Detection** 

Experiment 1 primarily evaluates vulnerable-versus-safe classification, not exact CWE taxonomy  matching. Several correct vulnerable detections had predicted CWEs that were related but not identical  to the benchmark CWE. For example, path traversal, access control, and credential-management families  often produced adjacent CWE IDs. This should be discussed as a taxonomy-mapping limitation rather  than a binary detection failure. 

**8\. Latency and Performance Analysis** 

The final architecture achieved an average latency of 49.755 seconds per case. This is a practical  improvement from earlier calibration runs where validation added latency comparable to detection.  Removing validation allowed the graph to execute the path Input \-\> Preprocess \-\> RAG \-\> Detection \-\> Fix  \-\> Output, reducing unnecessary repeated LLM calls. 

| Performance observation  | Evidence / interpretation |
| :---- | :---- |
| Average latency  | 49.755 seconds across 138 cases. |
| Safe-case speed  | Safe cases commonly completed in approximately 12-17  seconds because fix generation was skipped. |
| Vulnerable-case speed  | Vulnerable cases were generally slower because they triggered fix generation. |
| Long-tail outliers | CWE-347 vulnerable case took 1277.422 seconds; CWE-611 safe  took 338.958 seconds; CWE-99 vulnerable took 329.697  seconds. |
| Validation bypass impact | Validation consistency is recorded as 0.0 because the  validation node was bypassed, not because validation  disagreed. |

The latency distribution is therefore not uniform. Most cases completed quickly, but a small number of  high-latency outliers increased the average. These outliers likely reflect unusually long LLM reasoning or  fix-generation paths rather than RAG failure. Future work should impose model timeouts, maximum  token budgets, and possibly a no-fix mode for pure detection experiments. 

**9\. Fix Generation and Output Behavior** 

The final architecture generated fixes conditionally. If the detector classified a case as safe, the fix node  skipped repair generation. This design choice prevents unnecessary code rewrites, lowers API cost, and  shortens safe-case latency. For vulnerable classifications, the fix node attempted to generate repaired  Python code and a justification explaining how the fix removed the vulnerability while preserving  functionality. 

 Conditional fix generation proved efficient because many safe cases completed quickly after  detection. 

 False positives still triggered fix generation, which increases latency and can produce unnecessary  repairs; this is a consequence of prioritizing recall.

Experiment 1 Final Metrics Log \- LangGraph Security Auditing Tool   
 Some vulnerable detections did not generate fixes, likely due to API/model behavior or node-level  failure handling; this should be monitored in Experiment 3 when end-to-end repair is evaluated more directly. 

 Experiment 1 should be interpreted primarily as a detection experiment; fix quality is recorded but  not the central success metric. 

**10\. Design Choice Assessment** 

The final run provides evidence that several calibration decisions were effective. 

| Design choice  | Evidence from Experiment 1  | Assessment |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Full Hybrid RAG | All cases reported retrieval\_success \=  Yes; retrieval quality was usually Strong  or Moderate. | Effective; keep frozen. |
| OpenAI-aligned query embeddings | Removed Hugging Face loading   overhead and aligned query embeddings with stored OpenAI embeddings. | Effective for retrieval consistency and  runtime cleanliness. |
| Recall-oriented detector prompt  | False negatives fell to only 3 out of 69  vulnerable samples.  | Strongly effective for security priority. |
| Validation bypass | Average latency stabilized at 49.755  seconds and graph no longer pays a  second detector-like LLM call. | Effective; document as latency   optimization. |
| Fix skipped for safe samples  | Safe cases frequently completed in  roughly 12-17 seconds.  | Effective for cost and latency. |
| No Configuration C safeguard | Configuration C did not reduce false  positives and caused at least one   recovered vulnerable case to regress  during challenge testing. | Rejected; Configuration B remained the  winning prompt. |

**11\. Limitations and Future Improvements** 

 False positives remain the main limitation. Precision is strong but lower than recall because the  detector sometimes treats adjacent CWE evidence as sufficient risk. 

 The detector still struggles with a small number of broad or abstract vulnerability types, especially  CWE-20, CWE-414, and CWE-703. 

 Exact CWE mapping is imperfect even when binary vulnerable/safe classification is correct. A future  CWE-specialization module or taxonomy-aware reranker could improve this. 

 Validation was bypassed for final Experiment 1 speed. Future work should replace single-pass  validation with a cheaper deterministic validator, rule-based sanity checker, or selective validation  only for low-confidence cases. 

 Latency outliers should be controlled with timeout policies, output-token limits, and optional  detection-only mode for experiments focused on classification metrics. 

 RAG could be expanded with CVE examples, library-specific documentation, and family-level CWE  summaries for weak areas such as concurrency and exception handling. 

**12\. Final Assessment and Conclusions** 

Experiment 1 demonstrates that the calibrated LangGraph security auditing architecture performs  strongly across the full 69-CWE benchmark. The final architecture achieved 88.41% overall accuracy,  95.65% recall, and 89.19% F1. The low false-negative count is the strongest result: only three vulnerable 

Experiment 1 Final Metrics Log \- LangGraph Security Auditing Tool   
samples were missed. This supports the design goal of building a security assistant that prioritizes  vulnerability discovery over aggressive dismissal of possible risks. 

The main tradeoff is an elevated false-positive count. Thirteen safe samples were flagged as vulnerable,  often due to adjacent security concerns in access control, cryptography, credentials, or configuration.  This behavior is not ideal, but it is a defensible tradeoff for a detection assistant because false positives  can be reviewed manually, while false negatives allow vulnerabilities to remain unnoticed. 

The final conclusion is that the architecture is ready to be frozen for Experiment 1 and used as the basis  for comparative experiments against static analysis tools such as CodeQL and Bandit. The Experiment 1  results establish a strong baseline for the report: high recall, good overall accuracy, effective RAG  coverage, improved runtime after validation bypass, and clear areas for future precision-oriented  improvement.
